source_refs.note: Topic 2.5, printed page 29: why three quantum numbers are needed; the four are detailed in 2.5.1 to 2.5.3 and the spin topic.

blocks.text: The Bohr model was a one-dimensional model that used one quantum number to describe the distribution of electrons in the atom; the only important information was the size and energy of the orbit, described by the quantum number n. Schrodinger's model allows the electron to occupy three-dimensional space, so it needs three coordinates, three quantum numbers, to describe the orbitals in which electrons can be found. The three quantum numbers that come from Schrodinger's wave equations are the principal (n), angular (l) and magnetic (m) quantum numbers, which describe the size, shape and orientation in space of the orbitals in an atom. A fourth, the spin quantum number, distinguishes the two electrons that can share an orbital.

blocks.long_description: The principal quantum number n fixes the shell, its size and energy, and its capacity 2n squared. The azimuthal number l, from 0 to n minus 1, fixes the subshell and its shape: s spherical, p dumb-bell, d clover leaf, f complicated, holding 2(2l + 1) electrons. The magnetic number m, from minus l to plus l, gives the 2l + 1 orientations, so s has one orbital, p three, d five and f seven, all degenerate within a subshell. The spin number s is +1/2 or -1/2, and an orbital holds two electrons only if their spins are opposite. The nth shell has n subshells, n squared orbitals and 2n squared electrons.
